Quick answer up front: your biggest parcel, the **250 ML of Victorian Murray high-reliability shares (HRWS)**, is the one "allocation" usually means, so I've focused there. Here's the outlook.

**Where it stands now:** the Northern Victoria Resource Manager opened 2026-27 HRWS at **29%** on 1 July 2026, with about a 30% spill risk flagged and the next update due 15 July (NVRM/DEECA, as at 1 Jul 2026). Allocations climb through the season from that opening figure.

**Historical range for the finish:** across 31 seasons of Waterfind data, VIC Murray HRWS has finished at or near 100% in most years, the middle of the spread sitting right on **100%**, with the drier tail down around **95%** and wet years carrying surplus above (p90 near 200% counting spillable water). High-reliability shares get first call on inflows, so they tend to reach 100% even in ordinary years.

**What tilts it:** BOM/NSW DPIRD (issued 7 Jun 2026) have El Niño developing, roughly 80% through winter and near 90% into spring. El Niño leans drier over the southern Basin, which historically means a slower ratchet-up, so a soft, late climb is the main risk this year versus the usual push to 100%.

**What would change the view:** a wet late-winter/spring lifting Dartmouth-Hume inflows would accelerate it; a dry one keeps it grinding. Watch the 15 July and subsequent NVRM determinations.

Your other parcels sit on different paths, the Goulburn 1A and Murray "Low R" shares are low-reliability and climb far more slowly, and the SA and Murrumbidgee lines follow their own state determinations, so treat those separately if you want them.

For your Victorian Murray high-reliability shares, here's the picture. As at 1 July 2026 the current season (2026-27) opened at **29%** for VIC Murray HRWS (NVRM opening determination via the allocations snapshot). High-reliability shares are the most dependable class in the southern system, and historically they ratchet up strongly through the season.

Across 31 past VIC Murray HRWS seasons in the Waterfind record, the final allocation landed:

| Outcome | Final % |
|---|---:|
| Median (typical) | 100 |
| Lower quartile | 100 |
| 10th percentile (drier end) | 95 |
| Worst on record | 35 |

So in most seasons HRWS reaches 100% by year-end; the soft years are rare but real (2006-07 sat near 95%, and severe drought years have finished well below).

The one thing leaning against a fast climb this year: BOM's ENSO update (issued 7 June 2026) has El Niño developing over June-August with ~80% likelihood and persisting past November. El Niño seasons historically mean a slower allocation ratchet and firmer temporary-water prices across the southern Basin. That confidence is "reported", so worth checking the BOM ENSO page before you lean on it.

What would move the view: winter-spring inflows into Dartmouth/Hume and the next NVRM determinations. Verify the live figure with the Northern Victoria Resource Manager, since the opening % climbs with each announcement.

General information only, not financial or trading advice; ranges are historical Waterfind frequencies, not predictions.

If you want, I can run the same outlook for your Goulburn or Murrumbidgee holdings.

The band widens and lifts through spring, which is the usual seasonal pattern as irrigation demand builds.
